analytic.title: Scheduling and Analysis of Real-Time Tasks with Parallel Critical Sections

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Locks are the most widely used mechanisms to coordinate simultaneous accesses to exclusive shared resources. While locking protocols and associated schedulability analysis techniques have been extensively studied for sequential real-time tasks, work for parallel tasks largely lags behind. In the limited existing work on this topic, a common assumption is that a critical section must execute sequentially. However, this is not necessarily the case with parallel programming languages. In this paper, we study the analysis of parallel heavy real-time tasks (the density of which is greater than 1) with critical sections in parallel structures. We show that applying existing analysis techniques directly could be unsafe or much pessimistic for the considered model, and develop new techniques to address these problems. Comprehensive experiments are conducted to evaluate the performance of our method.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Time-critical applications are shifting from single-core to multicore platforms to meet the increasing requirements of high performance and low power consumption. Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAG) are widely used to model parallel workload and much work has been done in scheduling and analysis of DAG tasks recently [2,13,16].

Locking protocols are used to ensure mutually exclusive access to shared resources, which are essential to the design of correct and efficient real-time systems. While locking protocols for sequential real-time task systems are well-studied [1,5,8,12], the research on this topic for parallel real-time tasks is still at the early stage and subject to many limitations. In particular, a common assumption in all existing work on locking protocols for real-time parallel tasks [7,10,11,18] is that a critical section (a code segment that accesses the shared resource protected by locks) must be executed sequentially.

Unfortunately, the assumption of sequential critical sections does not always hold with parallel programming languages. For example, in OpenMP [14], the critical sections may have parallel structures. The pseudo-code of a parallel critical section (called PCS for short) is shown in Listing 1-the omp for directive specifies that the iterations of associated loops will be executed in parallel by the N threads created by the omp parallel directive. This parallel structure has already drawn some attention for accelerating the execution of critical sections. For example, speculative lock elision allows threads to execute critical sections concurrently [9], and different strategies for executing parallel critical sections are also proposed [15]. Although researches on parallel critical sections are still purely theoretical by now, we believe the study can significantly facilitate its implementation in a foreseeable future. Listing 1: An example of a PCS with OpenMP. Although the parallel critical sections provide possibility to improve real-time performance, the timing behavior of the system in the presence of PCS are more complex. Moreover, the existing analysis techniques cannot be simply extended and applied: considering a parallel critical section as a sequentially executed critical section is not safe whereas considering the parallel parts of a PCS as independent critical sections may be quite pessimistic. This problem will be discussed in details in Section 3. 3.

In this paper, we study the analysis of heavy real-time tasks with PCS protected by semaphores. More specifically, we first systematically analyze the problems when applying existing techniques (in which the execution of a critical section cannot be interrupted) on parallel real-time tasks with PCS, and then develop new techniques to safely bound the response times of heavy tasks with PCS (where the execution of a critical section can be interrupted at certain points). Experimental results show that our techniques consistently outperform the state-of-the-art under different parameter settings.

div.head: SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: In this paper, we consider a set of n tasks T = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n } executed on m identical processors ς = {ς 1 , ς 2 , ..., ς m } with n r shared resources Θ = {ℓ 1 , ..., ℓ n r }. Task Model. The workload structure of each task τ i is modeled by a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) G i = (V i , E i ), where V i represents the set of vertices, and E i represents the set of edges. A vertex is associated with a worst-case execution time (WCET) c(v). Each edge (u, v) ∈ E i represents the precedence relation between u and v, where u is a predecessor of v, and v is a successor of u. A path in G i is a sequence of vertices φ = {v 1 , v 2 , ...v p }, where v j is a predecessor of v j+1 for each pair of consecutive elements v j and v j+1 in φ. The length of a path φ is len(φ) = v ∈φ c(v).

A vertex with no predecessors (successors) is called a source (sink). Without loss of generality, we assume that G i has exactly one source and one sink 1 . The total worst-case execution time of all vertices of a task is denoted by C i = v ∈V i c(v). L i denotes the longest length among all paths in G i , i.e., L i = max ∀φ ∈G i len(φ). A path φ = {v x , ..., v y } is called a complete path if v x and v y correspond to the source and sink of G i , respectively. A DAG task τ i is shown in Fig. 1 where C i = 15 and L i = 8.

Each task τ i has a relative deadline D i and a period T i , where D i ≤ T i , i.e., tasks have constrained deadlines. The density of task τ i is δ i = C i /D i . At runtime, each task τ i generates a sequence of jobs which inherit the DAG structure G i of the task τ i . Let J i be an arbitrary job released by τ i , then r i and f i denote the release and finish times of J i , respectively. J i must finish no later than its absolute deadline r i + D i , and the subsequent job cannot arrive before r i + T i . The Worst-Case Response Time (WCRT) of task τ i is defined as
div.formula: R i = max ∀J i ∈τ i { f i -r i }. τ i is schedulable if R i ≤ D i . Resource Model. Each task τ i requests a set of resources Θ i ⊆ Θ.
div.p: Each resource ℓ q is protected by a binary semaphore (also called lock for simplicity). With a slight abuse of notation, we also use ℓ q to denote the lock protecting the resource ℓ q . A critical section of resource (or lock) ℓ q in τ i (denoted by Φ i,q ) is a code segment wrapped by a pair of lock request and lock release for ℓ q and is represented by a sub-graph of G i with exactly one source vertex (called the head of Φ i,q ) and one sink vertex (called the tail of Φ i,q ). The rest of the vertices in Φ i,q forms the body of Φ i,q . The head of Φ i,q can fork several body vertices that join together at the tail of Φ i,q . These body vertices can be executed in parallel. We use L(Φ i,q ) to denote the longest length among all paths in a particular critical section Φ i,q . And we define L i,q = max ∀Φ i,q ∈G i L(Φ i,q ) to denote the maximum L(Φ i,q ) among all Φ i,q ∈ G i . The total WCET of all vertices in Φ i,q is denoted by C(Φ i,q ), where C(Φ i,q ) = ∀v ∈Φ i,q c(v). Correspondingly, we define C i,q = max ∀Φ i,q ∈G i C(Φ i,q ) for τ i .

We use Φ to denote an arbitrary critical section. In particular, when we jointly consider several critical sections, Φ x (x = 1,2, ...) is used to distinguish among these critical sections. If a vertex is contained in Φ, it is called a critical vertex; otherwise, it is a normal vertex (i.e., the vertex does not belong to any critical section Φ). For example, as shown in Fig. 1, {v 2 , v 4 , v 5 , v 8 } forms the critical section Φ 1 in τ i : v 2 and v 8 are the head and tail of Φ 1 , respectively; v 4 and v 5 form the body of Φ 1 . And L(Φ 1 ) = 4, C(Φ 1 ) = 5.

A vertex v of J i is eligible if it has not completed its execution and all its predecessors of the same job J i have completed their execution. At run-time, an eligible vertex not executing is ready if it is a normal vertex or a lock-holding critical vertex. A ready vertex is available to be scheduled. A job suspends its execution when it needs to execute a critical section which is requesting a lock that is held by other critical sections. At this time, we say the critical section is suspended. A job J i requests ℓ q at most N i,q times. N φ i,q denotes the number of critical sections of ℓ q on a path φ and N t ot al i,q denotes the total number of critical vertices of ℓ q in τ i .

We say Φ i,q is satisfied when it holds ℓ q and is served when ∃v ∈ Φ i,q is executing. Φ i,q releases ℓ q when ∀v ∈ Φ i,q completes execution. For consistency, all vertices in Φ i,q are said to be holding ℓ q when Φ i,q is holding ℓ q . We assume that a critical section never requests another lock when holding a lock. 1 A DAG with multiple source (sink) vertices can be easily transferred to the required form by adding dummy vertices with zero WCET. Scheduling Paradigm. The task set T is scheduled by the federated scheduling paradigm [13]. Each heavy task τ i (δ i > 1) is off-line assigned with m i dedicated processors and all light tasks (δ i ≤ 1) are executed and scheduled together on a set of processors. At run-time, tasks are scheduled by a work-conserving scheduler, i.e., no processor is allowed to be idle if there is workload ready to be executed. We focus on heavy tasks in this paper since that the exclusive assignment for heavy tasks allows a simpler response time analysis due to contiguous service provided to tasks and the absence of inter-task interference (while the inter-and intra-task blocking can occur). Hence, we can focus better on the blocking analysis. The analysis of light tasks would be our future work.

div.p: It is evident that the use of PCS can shorten the length of the resource holding time, which is usually the system bottleneck from both the average-case and worst-case performance point of view and there may even exist circumstances under which the programmers have to implement code using PCS. In fact, we think implementing PCS is necessary to fully utilize the computing capacity of multiprocessors platforms with the support of parallel programming languages such as OpenMP when the PCS are carefully defined.

div.head: PRELIMINARY
div.p: To the best of our knowledge, the only work for analyzing realtime parallel task with semaphores is [11] and [18], where [18] considered a distributed system different from this paper. In the following, we first review the approach in [11] and then analyze the problems when it is directly applied on PCS.

div.head: LPP: Limited Pending Protocol
div.p: In [11], the limited pending protocol (LPP) was proposed for DAG tasks with shared resources protected by semaphores. In this paper, our focus is to present analysis for PCS rather than developing new locking protocols. So in the rest of this paper, we consider LPP as the adopted locking protocol.

Fig. 2 shows the transition of a critical section among different states under LPP (all the queues are FIFO queues). Under LPP, at any time, for ∀τ i and ∀ℓ q , the total number x of the critical sections in a task τ i which are either pending for or holding ℓ q is at most one. When x < 1, the first element in SQ q i (the suspended critical section queue of ℓ q in τ i ) is moved to the pending critical section queue of ℓ q PQ q ( 5 ○). The first element in PQ q obtains ℓ q and is moved to HQ i (the lock-holding critical section queue of τ i ) as soon as ℓ q becomes available ( 6○). When Φ is in HQ i , the vertices in Φ will be enqueued into V Q i (the ready critical vertex queue in τ i ) when they become eligible ( 7○), and waiting to be scheduled ( 8 ○).

div.head: Response Time Analysis Framework
div.p: In this section, we introduce some important concepts and properties which will be used in our analysis.

Definition 1. A key path of J i , denoted by λ = {v 1 , ..., v y }, is a complete path in G i , s.t., ∀j : 1 < j y, v j-1 is a predecessor of v j with the latest finish time among all predecessors of v j .
λ is said to be suspended by ℓ q if any vertex on λ requesting ℓ q is suspended. A processor is said to be busy when it is executing some vertex and busy with λ when it is executing some vertex on λ.
Let J i be an arbitrary job of τ i . The total amount of time on
div.formula: m i processors during [r i , f i ) is m i × (f i -r i ), which can be divided into three disjoint parts m i × (f i -r i ) = W i (λ) + P i (λ) + I i (λ):
div.p: • working time W i (λ): the cumulative length of time on m i processors spent on executing workload of J i . • po-blocking time P i (λ): the cumulative length of time on m i processors being idle when λ is suspended. • po-idle time I i (λ): the cumulative length of time on m i processors being idle when λ is not suspended. Based on the definition of po-blocking time, the upper bound of the WCRT of a task τ i given in [11] can be adopted: Lemma 1 ( [11]). For a task τ i , the WCRT can be bounded as R i ≤ (C i + (m i -1)L i + P i )/m i , where P i = max λ ∈τ i P i (λ).

By Lemma 1, the problem of bounding R i of τ i boils down to bounding P i (λ). Hence, the associated blocking analysis techniques should be developed for bounding P i (λ). We use P i,q (λ) to denote the po-blocking time when λ is suspended by a particular lock ℓ q , i.e., P i (λ) = ℓ q ∈Θ i P i,q (λ). Since λ could be suspended by at most one lock at any time, we further divide each P i,q (λ) into two parts:
• intra-task po-blocking time P I i,q (λ): the cumulative length of po-blocking time occurring on all processors when λ is suspended by ℓ q and ℓ q is held by τ i .
• inter-task po-blocking time P O i,q (λ): the cumulative length of po-blocking time occurring on all processors when λ is suspended by ℓ q and ℓ q is held by another task.
div.formula: P i (λ) = ℓ q ∈Θ i (P I i,q (λ) + P O i,q (λ))(1)

div.head: Problems of existing techniques
div.p: In the following, we show that existing techniques are not applicable on multi-vertex PCS. To safely use the computation power provided by the parallel programming framework in real-time environment, new techniques are required to support multi-vertex PCS. More specifically, there are mainly two reasons. Since the existing techniques can only address the analysis of single-vertex critical sections, to apply them to multi-vertex PCS, we need to model each PCS as single-vertex critical sections. A straightforward way is to model a PCS Φ as one critical vertex v with c(v) =C(Φ), as if all the vertices in Φ are executed sequentially. However, this approach is not safe, since the parallel critical sections of different resources may contend for the processors with more complex behavior, which may lead to even worse behavior than being executed sequentially. More specifically, suppose Φ is a critical section of ℓ q . The lock-holding time (after Φ starts) would be counted as C(Φ). However, at the boundaries of the vertices in Φ, all the processors could be busy with some other critical sections of ℓ k (k q), which could not be preempted, i.e., the actual lockholding time could be lager than C(Φ). Consequently, any other critical section waiting for ℓ q is transitively delayed, making the blocking analysis unsafe.

Another way is to consider each vertex of a PCS as an independent single-vertex critical section. However, this approach makes the blocking time analysis quite pessimistic. Intuitively, if each vertex v in a PCS Φ is considered as an individual single-vertex critical section, the lock can be preempted by other critical sections of the same resource, which would prolong the blocking time. This is not the case when we address the analysis of a PCS Φ with the assumption that Φ will not release the lock until ∀v ∈ Φ completes.
In summary, extending the existing blocking analysis techniques to our considered model is not a trivial step, and new blocking time analysis techniques must be developed for multi-vertex PCS.

div.head: BLOCKING ANALYSIS FOR PCS
div.p: In this section, we develop blocking analysis techniques for PCS. We first introduce some relevant concept and properties of a critical section. Then, we analyze the po-blocking time for each task.

div.head: Ready-waiting Time Window
div.p: Note that under LPP, when a vertex v ∈ Φ i,q becomes eligible and is enqueued into V Q i , it may not start executing immediately ( 8 ○ in Fig. 2): (1) it must wait in V Q i until its turn; (2) even if v is in the first position in V Q i , it has to wait for an available processor. Hence, we first define the ready-waiting time window of Φ: Definition 2. For a critical section Φ i,q , we use Λ i,q to denote the ready-waiting time window of Φ i,q : Λ i,q consists of the set of time intervals during which ℓ q is held by Φ i,q , and there exists some vertex v in Φ i,q which is ready but not executing.

We use the execution of an arbitrary 8-vertex critical section Φ to illustrate the ready-waiting time window Λ of Φ. Fig. 3 i.e., there are ready vertices waiting to be scheduled during [t 3 , t 6 ). Hence, by Definition 2, [t 3 , t 6 ) also belongs to Λ, although there are some vertices in Φ being executed. Considering that Φ may either be not served or served during Λ, we have the following lemma: Lemma 2. At any time point during the ready-waiting time window Λ i,q of critical section Φ i,q from τ i , all m i processors must be executing some critical sections of some other resource than ℓ q from τ i or some body vertices in Φ i,q .

Proof. By Definition 2, there must be v ∈ Φ i,q in V Q i ( 7 ○ in Fig. 2) waiting to be scheduled during Λ i,q . If there is any processor being idle or executing a normal vertex preemptively, the ready vertex v in Φ i,q must start its execution ( 8○ in Fig. 2). Hence, all m i processors must be busy with some critical vertices that cannot be preempted by v. Since Φ i,q is holding ℓ q , no other critical sections can hold ℓ q and execute. Hence, the lemma is proved. □

Since the body of Φ may not start execution at the same time, we introduce the concept of z-th group body of Φ: Definition 3. The body of a critical section Φ can be executed in z groups, where we say that the body vertices with the same start time of execution are in the same group. These z groups are sorted in an increasing order of the start time of the group. The z-th group body is then the group of body vertices with the latest start time.
In Fig. 3, the body of Φ is executed in z = 4 groups, which are {v 2 ,v 3 }, {v 5 ,v 6 }, {v 4 } and {v 7 } (the z-th group body), respectively.

Note that the concrete z groups depend on the number of available processors (which are either idle or preemptively executing some normal vertices in τ i ) at run-time, which cannot be known beforehand. However, z groups are only used for simplicity of the presentation of the proof, which do not need to be calculated-this will be shown in the proof of the following lemmas. Lemma 3. Suppose the body of a critical section Φ is executed in z groups. Let K denote the set of time intervals iv where: iv Λ and in ∀iv ∈ K, Φ is holding the lock. During K, one of the head of Φ, the tail of Φ and the z-th group body of Φ must be executing.

Proof. We use H to denote the set of time intervals during which Φ is holding the lock. Apparently, H = K ∪ Λ. During ∀iv ∈ H , if the head, the tail and the z-th group body of Φ are all not executing, we must have iv ∈ Λ, i.e., iv K, which means the contrapositive of the lemma is true. Hence, the lemma is proved. □

Based on Lemma 3, the cumulative length of such time interval set K can be bounded. Lemma 4. Let Φ i,q be one critical section of ℓ q in task τ i and Λ i,q denote its ready-waiting time window. Let K i,q denote the set of time intervals iv where Φ i,q is holding ℓ q during ∀iv and iv Λ i,q . The cumulative length |K i,q | of K i,q can be bounded as: |K i,q | ≤ L i,q .

Proof. By Lemma 3, one of the head, the tail and the z-th group body of Φ must be executing during K i,q , which corresponds to a path in Φ i,q . So for each critical section Φ i,q , the cumulative length of all the time intervals that belong to K i,q is at most L i,q . □

div.head: PO-blocking Analysis for PCS
div.p: Now we develop blocking analysis techniques for PCS. Our focus is to safely bound P I i,q (λ) and P O i,q (λ), respectively. Based on the properties of the ready-waiting time window, we can bound P I i,q (λ) by the following lemma. Lemma 5. P I i,q (λ) ≤ U I (N λ i,q ), where
div.formula: U I (N λ i,q ) = min{N λ i,q , 1} • (N i,q -N λ i,q )(m i -1)L i,q
div.p: Proof. we consider two cases: (1) N λ i,q = 0: there are no critical sections of ℓ q on λ and λ will not be suspended by ℓ q . Hence, P I i,q (λ) = 0, the lemma holds. (2) N λ i,q > 0: Let K i,q denote the set of time intervals iv where: during ∀iv, λ is suspended by ℓ q which is held by a critical section Φ i,q in τ i and iv Λ i,q (the ready-waiting time window of Φ i,q ). By Lemma 2, during Λ i,q , all m i processors must be busy so that no P I i,q (λ) occurs, i.e., P I i,q (λ) only occurs during K i,q . By Lemma 3, the maximum intra-task po-blocking time in each time unit in K i,q is (m i -1): only one processor is executing Φ i,q (executing one of the head, the tail or the z-th group body with at least one vertex), while the remaining m i -1 processors are all idle. Hence, P I i,q (λ) ≤ (m i -1)(|K i,q |). By Lemma 4, for each Φ i,q , the total length of the time intervals that does not belong to Λ i,q is at most L i,q . Since λ must execute sequentially and there are at most (N i,q -N λ i,q ) critical sections not on λ, we have | K i,q | ≤ (N i,q -N λ i,q )L i,q . Hence, P I i,q (λ) ≤ (N i,q -N λ i,q )(m i -1)L i,q . From the above, the lemma holds for both cases. □ In the following, we bound the inter-task po-blocking time P O i,q (λ). div.head: EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, we systematically evaluate the performance of our presented analysis technique (denoted by SEM) with the following state-of-art analysis methods:
• SPIN: test for FIFO spin locks in [7].
• POMLP: the POMLP protocol for semaphores in [10].
• POMIP: the POMIP protocol for semaphores in [10].
• LPP: the LPP protocol for semaphores in [11].
• DPCP-p: the DPCP-p protocol for semaphores in [18].

• FED: the original schedulability test of federated scheduling [13] without considering shared resources. These methods can be applied to PCS by considering each vertex of a PCS as an independent single-vertex critical section (as introduced in Section 3.3), i.e., J i requests ℓ q at most N t ot al i,q times. The experimental parameters are generated as follows: Task: For each task τ i , the DAG structure of τ i was generated by the Erdös-Rényi method [6], where the number of vertices |V i | was randomly chosen in [200,400], and the probability of an edge between any two vertices was set to 0.1. The WCET of each vertex is randomly picked in [300, 1500] (these metrics are consistent with the measurement results of realistic OpenMP programs in [17]). The deadline D i of each task τ i is generated in a similar way with that DAC '22, July 10-14, 2022, San Francisco, CA, USA Yang Wang and Xu Jiang, et al.

in [7]: after L i is fixed, D i is generated according to a ratio L i /D i randomly chosen in [0.125, 0.25]. The period T i = D i . Each task τ i is set to be a light task with a probability of 1/3 3 . In the processor allocation procedure, each light task τ i is initially assigned one dedicated processor rather than sharing processors with other light tasks as specified by the original federated scheduling, so that our presented analysis technique can be applied. Resource: The number of resource types n r is in [1,20]. The number of critical sections of each resource from all tasks τ i ∈ T N i,q is in [10,440]. We set max ∀τ i {L i,q } to be in the range [5,160] and each L i,q is randomly picked in [5, max ∀τ i {L i,q }]. For each τ i and each ℓ q , we randomly chose N i,q × µ critical sections as PCS with 4-7 vertices and the remaining critical sections are single-vertex ones. All critical sections are randomly distributed to the vertices.

For each task set, we generate n ∈ [2, 15] tasks. For each group of experiment, the normalized utilization U norm (U norm = U /m) of the task set T is predefined. After we generate all the tasks in T , we can compute the utilization U of T ; then, we set the number of processors according to the formula m = ⌈ U U nor m ⌉. In Fig. 4 (a)-(f), we set a basic configuration (U norm = 0.4, n r = 6, τ i ∈ T N i,q = 250, max ∀τ i {L i,q } = 110, n = 3, µ = 0.2) and vary one parameter with the others unchanged in each group. For each configuration (one point on the X-axis), we generate 1000 task sets.

It can be observed that the performance of SEM consistently outperforms the other tests. The main reason is that we jointly analyze the vertices in a parallel critical section Φ and only the longest path in Φ needs to be considered. But for all the other tests, where the vertices in Φ are considered as separate critical sections, every vertex is analyzed individually so that the vertices in Φ may experience much more blocking-not only the vertices in 3 We repeatedly generate D i until δ i ≤ 1 holds when a light task is expected.

Φ may be blocked at every vertex boundary, but also increases the number of critical sections that content for the same resource with it. Moreover, we can observe from Fig. 4(f) that the gap between SEM and other tests enlarges with higher µ, since the number of critical sections grows as µ grows under these tests while it does not change under SEM.

div.head: CONCLUSIONS AND DISCUSSIONS
div.p: In this paper, we study the analysis of parallel real-time tasks with PCS. We show that applying existing analysis techniques could be unsafe or much pessimistic for the considered model, and develop new techniques to address these problems. We focus on heavy tasks in this work. However, our blocking analysis techniques can be easily extended for systems consisting of both heavy and light tasks. The processors where all light tasks are scheduled can be regarded as a cluster such that cluster-based locking protocol like OMLP can be applied. The only concern is the inter-blocking between light tasks and heavy tasks which can be addressed by extending the analysis techniques introduced in this paper-this will be our future work. Although the blocking analysis in this paper could not be directly applied on other scheduling algorithms, the intuition behind it is still inspiring. The key part of blocking analysis under other scheduling is that we need to carefully define different blocking times. Besides the adopted scheduling algorithms, the applied locking protocol to coordinate resource accesses would make a big difference in the blocking analysis as well. Specifically, since the tasks need to share the processors under other scheduling, the traditional pi-blocking time as well as the transitive pi-blocking time must be considered as in [4].
